title: Chapter 17 — Principal Causes Maintaining The Democratic Republic In The United States
paragraphs: Principal Causes Which Tend to Maintain the Democratic Republic in the United States

A democratic republic exists in the United States, and the main purpose of this book has been to account for its existence. Several of the causes that help sustain the institutions of America have been passed over or only hinted at as I was carried along by my subject. Others I have been unable to discuss, and those I have dwelt on most are, so to speak, buried in the details of the earlier parts of this work. Before I go on to speak of the future, therefore, I think I cannot do better than gather together, in a small compass, the reasons that best explain the present. In this retrospective chapter I shall be brief, taking care only to remind the reader, very summarily, of what he already knows; and I shall select only the most prominent of those facts I have not yet pointed out.
All the causes that contribute to the maintenance of the democratic republic in the United States can be reduced to three heads:—
I. The peculiar and accidental situation in which Providence has placed the Americans.
III. The manners and customs of the people.

Accidental or Providential Causes that Contribute to the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States: The Union has no neighbors—No metropolis—The Americans have had the chances of birth in their favor—America an empty country—How this circumstance powerfully contributes to the maintenance of the democratic republic in America—How the American wilds are peopled—The eagerness of the Anglo-Americans to take possession of the solitudes of the New World—Influence of physical prosperity on the political opinions of the Americans.

A thousand circumstances, independent of human will, combine to make it easier to sustain a democratic republic in the United States. Some of these peculiarities are well known; others can be easily pointed out; but I shall limit myself to the most prominent among them.

The Americans have no neighbors, and so they have no great wars, financial crises, invasions, or conquests to dread. They need neither heavy taxes nor large armies nor great generals, and they have nothing to fear from a scourge more formidable to republics than all these evils combined: military glory. It is impossible to deny the inconceivable influence that military glory exerts on the spirit of a nation. General Jackson, whom the Americans have twice elected to head their Government, is a man of violent temper and mediocre talents; nothing in the whole course of his career ever showed him qualified to govern a free people, and indeed the majority of the enlightened classes of the Union has always been opposed to him. Yet he was raised to the Presidency, and has been kept in that lofty station, solely by the memory of a victory he won twenty years ago under the walls of New Orleans—a victory that was, however, a very ordinary achievement, and that could only be remembered in a country where battles are rare. The people thus carried away by the illusions of glory is unquestionably the coldest and most calculating, the most unmilitary (if I may use the word), and the most prosaic of all the peoples of the earth.

America has no great capital city whose influence is felt, directly or indirectly, across the whole country, and I consider this one of the chief causes that sustain republican institutions in the United States. In cities, men cannot be prevented from gathering together and stirring each other into sudden and passionate resolutions. Cities may be seen as large assemblies in which every inhabitant is a member; their populace exerts an enormous influence on the magistrates, and often carries out its own wishes without their intervention.

a [ The United States has no metropolis, but it already contains several very large cities. Philadelphia counted 161,000 inhabitants and New York 202,000 in 1830. The lower classes who inhabit these cities form a rabble even more formidable than the populace of European towns. They consist, in the first place, of freed blacks, who are condemned by the laws and by public opinion to a hereditary state of misery and degradation. They also contain a multitude of Europeans driven to the shores of the New World by misfortune or misconduct; and these men inoculate the United States with all our vices, without bringing with them any of the interests that might counteract their baneful influence. As inhabitants of a country where they have no civil rights, they are ready to turn every passion that stirs the community to their own advantage; and so, within the last few months, serious riots have broken out in Philadelphia and New York. Disturbances of this kind are unknown in the rest of the country, which is in no way alarmed by them, because the city population has so far exerted neither power nor influence over the rural districts. Nevertheless, I regard the size of certain American cities, and especially the nature of their population, as a real danger threatening the future security of the democratic republics of the New World; and I venture to predict that they will perish from this cause unless the government manages to create an armed force that, while it remains under the control of the national majority, will be independent of the city population and able to repress its excesses.

[The population of the city of New York had risen, by 1870, to 942,292, and that of Philadelphia to 674,022. Brooklyn, which may be said to form part of New York City, has a population of 396,099 in addition to New York's own. The frequent disturbances in the great cities of America, and the excessive corruption of their local governments—over which there is no effective control—are among the greatest evils and dangers of the country.]]

To subject the provinces to the metropolis is therefore not only to place the fate of the empire in the hands of one part of the community, which may be condemned as unjust, but to place it in the hands of a populace acting on its own impulses, which must be avoided as dangerous. The dominance of capital cities is therefore a serious blow to the representative system, and it exposes modern republics to the same defect that destroyed the republics of antiquity, which all perished because they did not know this form of government.

It would be easy for me to list many secondary causes that have helped establish, and now help maintain, the democratic republic of the United States. But among these favorable elements I discern two principal ones, which I hasten to point out. I have already observed that the origin of the American settlements may be seen as the first and most effective cause to which the present prosperity of the United States can be attributed. The Americans had the chances of birth in their favor, and their forefathers brought with them the equality of conditions from which the democratic republic has naturally grown. Nor was this all they did: besides this republican social condition, the early settlers bequeathed to their descendants those customs, manners, and opinions that most contribute to the success of a republican form of government. When I reflect on the consequences of this primary circumstance, it seems to me that I see the destiny of America embodied in the first Puritan who landed on those shores, just as the whole human race was represented by the first man.

The chief circumstance that has favored the establishment and maintenance of a democratic republic in the United States is the nature of the territory the Americans inhabit. Their ancestors gave them the love of equality and of freedom, but God himself gave them the means of remaining equal and free, by placing them on a boundless continent open to their efforts. General prosperity is favorable to the stability of all governments, but especially of a democratic constitution, which depends on the disposition of the majority, and above all of that part of the community most exposed to the pressure of want. When the people rules, it must be made happy, or it will overturn the State; and misery can drive it to the same excesses to which ambition drives kings. The physical causes, independent of the laws, that help promote general prosperity, are more numerous in America than they have ever been in any other country in the world, at any other period of history. In the United States, not only is the legislation democratic—nature herself favors the cause of the people.

In what part of human history can we find anything like what is happening before our eyes in North America? The celebrated communities of antiquity were all founded in the midst of hostile nations, which they had to subdue before they could flourish in their place. Even the moderns have found, in parts of South America, vast regions inhabited by peoples of inferior civilization, who nevertheless occupied and cultivated the soil. To found their new states, they had to wipe out or subjugate a large population, until civilization was made to blush for its success. But North America was inhabited only by wandering tribes, who took no thought of the natural riches of the soil; and that vast country was still, strictly speaking, an empty continent, a deserted land awaiting its inhabitants.

Everything is extraordinary in America—the social condition of the inhabitants as well as the laws; but the soil on which these institutions are founded is more extraordinary than all the rest. When man was first placed on the earth by the Creator, the earth was inexhaustible in its youth, but man was weak and ignorant; and when he had learned to uncover the treasures it contained, hosts of his fellow creatures covered its surface, and he was forced to win an asylum of rest and freedom by the sword. At that same moment North America was discovered, as if it had been held in reserve by the Deity, and had just risen from beneath the waters of the deluge.

That continent still shows, as it did in the earliest time, rivers flowing from never-failing sources, green and moist solitudes, and fields that the farmer's plow has never turned. In this state it is offered to man—not to man in the barbarous and isolated condition of the early ages, but to a being already in possession of the most potent secrets of the natural world, united to his fellow-men, and instructed by the experience of fifty centuries. At this very moment, thirteen million civilized Europeans are peacefully spreading over those fertile plains, whose resources and extent they do not yet themselves accurately know. Three or four thousand soldiers drive the wandering races of the natives before them; they are followed by the pioneers, who cut through the woods, scare off the beasts of prey, trace the courses of the inland streams, and prepare the triumphal advance of civilization across the wilderness.

The favorable influence that America's material prosperity has on the institutions of that country has been described so often by others, and mentioned so often by myself, that I shall not dwell on it beyond adding a few facts. A mistaken notion is generally held that the deserts of America are peopled by European emigrants who disembark every year on the shores of the New World, while the American population grows and multiplies on the soil its forefathers tilled. But the European settler usually arrives in the United States without friends, and sometimes without resources; to survive, he is forced to work for hire, and he rarely moves beyond that belt of industrious population next to the ocean. The desert cannot be explored without capital or credit, and the body must be seasoned to the rigors of a new climate before it can be exposed to the hazards of forest life. It is the Americans themselves who daily leave the places of their birth to acquire extensive domains in a remote country. Thus the European leaves his cottage for the trans-Atlantic shores, and the American, born on that very coast, plunges in his turn into the wilds of Central America. This double emigration is unceasing: it begins in the remotest parts of Europe, it crosses the Atlantic Ocean, and it advances across the solitudes of the New World. Millions of men are marching at once toward the same horizon; their language, their religion, their manners differ, but their object is the same. The gifts of fortune are promised in the West, and to the West they bend their course. *b

b [ [The number of foreign immigrants into the United States in the last fifty years (from 1820 to 1871) is stated to be 7,556,007. Of these, 4,104,553 spoke English—that is, they came from Great Britain, Ireland, or the British colonies; 2,643,069 came from Germany or northern Europe; and about half a million from the south of Europe.]]

No event can be compared with this continuous transplantation of the human race except, perhaps, the invasions that preceded the fall of the Roman Empire. Then, as now, generations of men were driven forward in the same direction to meet and struggle on the same ground; but the designs of Providence were not the same. Then, every newcomer was a harbinger of destruction and death; now, every adventurer brings with him the elements of prosperity and life. The future still hides from us the longer-term consequences of this migration of Americans toward the West, but we can easily see its more immediate results. Because a portion of the inhabitants leave every year the States in which they were born, the population of those States increases very slowly, even though they have long been settled. Thus in Connecticut, which has only fifty-nine inhabitants per square mile, the population has grown by only about a quarter in forty years, while England's has grown by a third in the same period. The European emigrant therefore always lands in a country that is only half full, where hands are in demand: he becomes a workman in comfortable circumstances; his son goes to seek his fortune in unsettled regions and becomes a rich landowner. The former amasses the capital that the latter invests, and neither the newcomer nor the native knows want.

The laws of the United States are extremely favorable to the division of property, but a cause more powerful than the laws prevents property from being divided to excess. *c This is very noticeable in the States that are beginning to be densely peopled. Massachusetts is the most populous part of the Union, yet it has only eighty inhabitants per square mile—far fewer than in France, which counts 162 on the same area. But in Massachusetts estates are very rarely divided; the eldest son takes the land, and the others go to seek their fortune in the desert. The law has abolished the rights of primogeniture, but circumstances have combined to restore it in a form about which no one can complain, and by which no just rights are harmed.
c [ In New England the estates are exceedingly small, but they are rarely subjected to further division.]

A single fact will be enough to show the enormous number of individuals who leave New England in this way to settle in the wilds. We were assured in 1830 that thirty-six members of Congress had been born in the small State of Connecticut. Connecticut's population, which makes up only one forty-third of that of the United States, thus supplied one-eighth of the whole body of representatives. Yet the State of Connecticut itself sends only five delegates to Congress; the other thirty-one sit for the new Western States. If these thirty-one men had stayed in Connecticut, it is probable that instead of becoming rich landowners they would have remained humble laborers, that they would have lived in obscurity without being able to rise into public life, and that, far from becoming useful members of the legislature, they might have turned into unruly citizens.

These reflections do not escape the Americans any more than they escape us. "It cannot be doubted," says Chancellor Kent in his Treatise on American Law, "that the division of landed estates must produce great evils when it is carried to such excess that each parcel of land is insufficient to support a family; but these disadvantages have never been felt in the United States, and many generations must pass before they can be felt. The extent of our inhabited territory, the abundance of adjacent land, and the continual stream of emigration flowing from the shores of the Atlantic toward the interior of the country, are enough for now, and will long remain enough, to prevent the excessive parceling of estates."

It is difficult to describe the eagerness with which the American rushes forward to seize the immense prize that fortune holds out to him. In the chase he fearlessly braves the Indian's arrow and the fevers of the forest; he is unmoved by the silence of the woods; the approach of beasts of prey does not disturb him—for he is driven on by a passion more intense than the love of life. Before him lies a boundless continent, and he presses on as if time were pressing, as if he were afraid of finding no room for his efforts. I have spoken of the emigration from the older States, but how shall I describe the one that takes place from the newer ones? Barely fifty years have passed since the State of Ohio was founded; most of its inhabitants were not born within its borders; its capital has stood for only thirty years, and its territory is still covered by an immense stretch of uncultivated fields. Yet the population of Ohio is already pushing westward, and most of the settlers who come down into the fertile savannahs of Illinois are citizens of Ohio. These men left their first country to improve their condition; they leave their resting-place to improve it still more. Fortune awaits them everywhere, but happiness eludes them. The desire for prosperity has become in their minds an ardent and restless passion that grows by what it gains. Early on, they broke the ties that bound them to their native earth, and they have formed no new ones on their way. Emigration was at first a necessity for them, a means of subsistence; but it soon becomes a sort of game of chance, which they pursue as much for the excitement it stirs as for the gain it brings.

Sometimes man's progress is so rapid that the desert reappears behind him. The woods bow to let him pass, and spring up again when he has gone. It is not uncommon, in crossing the new States of the West, to come upon deserted dwellings in the midst of the wilds; the traveler often finds the remains of a log house in the most solitary retreats—remains that bear witness both to the power and to the fickleness of man. In these abandoned fields, over these one-day ruins, the primeval forest soon scatters fresh vegetation; the beasts resume the haunts that were once their own; and Nature covers the traces of man's path with branches and flowers that wipe out his fleeting track.

I remember that, in crossing one of the woodland districts that still cover the State of New York, I reached the shores of a lake set deep in forests as old as the world. A small island, covered with woods whose thick foliage hid its banks, rose from the center of the waters. On the shores of the lake nothing pointed to the presence of man except a column of smoke that could be seen on the horizon, rising from the treetops to the clouds and seeming to hang from heaven rather than to be climbing toward the sky. An Indian canoe had been hauled up on the sand, and it tempted me to visit the little island that had first caught my eye; in a few minutes I set foot on its banks. The whole island formed one of those delightful solitudes of the New World which almost make civilized man regret the haunts of the savage. A luxuriant vegetation bore witness to the incomparable fruitfulness of the soil. The deep silence common to the wilds of North America was broken only by the hoarse cooing of the wood-pigeon and the tapping of the woodpecker on the bark of the trees. I was far from supposing that this spot had ever been inhabited, so completely did Nature seem to have been left to her own whims; but when I reached the center of the island, I thought I saw some traces of man. I then examined the surrounding objects carefully, and I soon realized that a European had undoubtedly come to seek refuge in this retreat. Yet what changes had taken place in the scene of his labors! The logs he had hastily cut to build himself a shed had sprouted afresh; the very props were intertwined with living greenery, and his cabin had been turned into a bower. Among these shrubs a few stones could be seen, blackened with fire and sprinkled with thin ash—here the hearth had no doubt been, and the falling chimney had covered it in rubble. I stood for some time in silent admiration of the exuberance of Nature and the littleness of man; and when I had to leave that enchanting solitude, I exclaimed sadly, "Are ruins, then, already here?"

In Europe we tend to regard a restless disposition, an unbounded desire for riches, and an excessive love of independence as tendencies very dangerous to society. Yet these are the very elements that secure a long and peaceful existence for the republics of America. Without these restless passions, the population would collect in certain spots and would soon be subject to wants like those of the Old World, which are hard to satisfy; for such is the present good fortune of the New World that the vices of its inhabitants are scarcely less favorable to society than their virtues. These circumstances exert a great influence on how human actions are judged in the two hemispheres. The Americans often call what we would call cupidity a praiseworthy industry, and they blame as faint-heartedness what we regard as the virtue of moderate desires.

In France, simple tastes, orderly manners, domestic affections, and the attachment men feel to the place of their birth are seen as great guarantees of the peace and happiness of the State. But in America nothing seems more harmful to society than these virtues. The French Canadians, who have faithfully preserved the traditions of their original manners, are already short of room on their small territory; and this little community, which has only recently begun to exist, will soon fall prey to the calamities that afflict old nations. In Canada, the most enlightened, patriotic, and humane inhabitants make extraordinary efforts to make the people dissatisfied with the simple enjoyments that still content them. There, the seductions of wealth are extolled with as much zeal as the charms of an honest but modest income are praised in the Old World, and more effort is spent exciting the passions of the citizens there than calming them elsewhere. If we listen to their eulogies, we shall hear that nothing is more praiseworthy than to exchange the pure and homely pleasures that even the poor man tastes in his own country for the dull delights of prosperity under a foreign sky; to leave the family hearth and the turf beneath which one's forefathers sleep; in short, to abandon the living and the dead in search of fortune.

At present America offers a field for human effort far larger than any amount of labor that can be applied to work it. In America too much knowledge cannot be spread; for all knowledge, while it may serve the one who possesses it, also benefits those who do not. New wants are not to be feared, since they can be satisfied without difficulty; the growth of human passions need not be dreaded, since all passions can find an easy and a legitimate object; nor can men be given too much freedom, since they are scarcely ever tempted to misuse their liberties.

The American republics of the present day are like companies of adventurers formed to explore together the wastelands of the New World and to carry on a flourishing trade. The passions that stir the Americans most deeply are not their political but their commercial passions—or, to put it more accurately, they carry the habits they form in business into their political life. They love order, without which affairs do not prosper, and they set a special value on regular conduct, which is the foundation of solid business. They prefer the good sense that amasses large fortunes to the enterprising spirit that often squanders them; general ideas alarm their minds, which are used to positive calculations, and they hold practice in higher honor than theory.

It is in America that one learns to understand the influence that physical prosperity exerts on political actions, and even on opinions that should acknowledge no master but reason; and this truth is most visible among foreigners. Most of the European emigrants to the New World carry with them that wild love of independence and of change that our calamities are so apt to breed. I sometimes met Europeans in the United States who had been forced to leave their own country because of their political opinions. They all astonished me by the language they used, but one of them surprised me more than all the rest. As I was crossing one of the most remote districts of Pennsylvania, I was caught by nightfall and had to beg for hospitality at the gate of a wealthy planter, a Frenchman by birth. He invited me to sit down by his fire, and we began to talk with that freedom that suits people who meet in the backwoods, two thousand leagues from their native country. I knew that my host had been a great leveler and an ardent demagogue forty years earlier, and that his name was not unknown to fame. I was therefore more than a little surprised to hear him discuss the rights of property as an economist or a landowner might have done: he spoke of the necessary gradations that fortune establishes among men, of obedience to the established laws, of the influence of good morals in commonwealths, and of the support that religious opinions give to order and to freedom. He even went so far as to quote an evangelical authority in support of one of his political tenets.

I listened, and marveled at the feebleness of human reason. A proposition is true or false, but no art can prove it to be one or the other amid the uncertainties of science and the conflicting lessons of experience—until some new incident disperses the clouds of doubt. I was poor, I become rich, and I am not to expect that prosperity will act on my conduct and leave my judgment free; my opinions change with my fortune, and the happy circumstances I turn to my advantage supply me with the decisive argument that was missing before. The influence of prosperity acts even more freely on the American than on foreigners. The American has always seen the connection between public order and public prosperity—intimately united as they are—unfolding before his eyes; he cannot conceive of one existing without the other; he has therefore nothing to forget, nor has he, like so many Europeans, to unlearn the lessons of his early education.
Influence of the Laws on the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States
Three principal causes of the maintenance of the democratic republic—Federal Constitution—Municipal institutions—Judicial power.

The main aim of this book has been to make known the laws of the United States. If this purpose has been accomplished, the reader is already in a position to judge for himself which are the laws that really tend to maintain the democratic republic, and which ones endanger its existence. If I have not succeeded in making this clear across the whole course of my work, I cannot hope to do so within the limits of a single chapter. I do not intend to retrace the path I have already followed, and a very few lines will suffice to recapitulate what I have previously explained.
Three circumstances seem to me to contribute most powerfully to the maintenance of the democratic republic in the United States.
The first is the Federal form of Government the Americans have adopted, which enables the Union to combine the power of a great empire with the security of a small State.
The second consists in the municipal institutions that limit the despotism of the majority, and at the same time give the people a taste for freedom and a knowledge of the art of being free.

The third is to be found in the constitution of the judicial power. I have shown how the courts of justice serve to check the excesses of democracy, and how they restrain and guide the impulses of the majority without halting its activity.
Influence of Manners on the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States

I have previously remarked that the manners of the people may be considered one of the general causes to which the maintenance of a democratic republic in the United States is due. I used the word manners here in the sense the ancients gave to mores, for I apply it not only to manners in the proper sense—what makes up the character of social intercourse—but I extend it to the various notions and opinions current among men, and to the mass of ideas that make up their cast of mind. I include under this term, therefore, the whole moral and intellectual condition of a people. My intention is not to paint a picture of American manners, but simply to point out those features of them that are favorable to the maintenance of political institutions.
Religion Considered as a Political Institution, Which Powerfully Contributes to the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic Among the Americans

North America peopled by men who professed a democratic and republican Christianity—Arrival of the Catholics—Why the Catholics form the most democratic and the most republican class at the present time.

Every religion is found alongside a political opinion connected to it by affinity. If the human mind is left to follow its own bent, it will regulate the temporal and spiritual institutions of society on one uniform principle, and man will try, if I may put it this way, to bring the state in which he lives on earth into harmony with the state he believes awaits him in heaven. The greater part of British America was peopled by men who, having shaken off the authority of the Pope, acknowledged no other religious supremacy; they brought with them into the New World a form of Christianity which I cannot better describe than by calling it a democratic and republican religion. This sect contributed powerfully to the establishment of a democracy and a republic, and from the earliest settlement of the emigrants onward, politics and religion entered into an alliance that has never been dissolved.

About fifty years ago Ireland began to pour a Catholic population into the United States; on the other hand, the Catholics of America made converts, and at present more than a million Christians professing the truths of the Church of Rome are to be found in the Union. *d The Catholics are faithful to the observances of their religion; they are fervent and zealous in defending and believing its doctrines. Nevertheless they form the most republican and the most democratic class of citizens in the United States; and although this fact may surprise the observer at first, the causes behind it can easily be discovered on reflection.

d [ [It is difficult to ascertain accurately the size of the Roman Catholic population of the United States, but in 1868 an able writer in the Edinburgh Review (vol. cxxvii. p. 521) affirmed that the whole Catholic population of the United States was then about 4,000,000, divided into 43 dioceses, with 3,795 churches, under the care of 45 bishops and 2,317 clergymen. But this rapid increase is mainly supported by immigration from the Catholic countries of Europe.]]

I think the Catholic religion has been wrongly regarded as the natural enemy of democracy. Among the various sects of Christians, Catholicism seems to me, on the contrary, to be one of those most favorable to the equality of conditions. In the Catholic Church the religious community is made up of only two elements: the priest and the people. The priest alone rises above the rank of his flock, and all below him are equal.

On points of doctrine the Catholic faith places all human capacities on the same level; it subjects the wise and the ignorant, the man of genius and the vulgar crowd, to the details of the same creed; it imposes the same observances on the rich and the poor, inflicts the same austerities on the strong and the weak, admits no compromise with mortal man, but, reducing the whole human race to the same standard, merges all the distinctions of society at the foot of the same altar, just as they are merged in the sight of God. If Catholicism predisposes the faithful to obedience, it certainly does not prepare them for inequality; the opposite may be said of Protestantism, which generally tends to make men independent more than it tends to make them equal.

Catholicism is like an absolute monarchy: if the sovereign is removed, all the other classes of society are more equal than they are in republics. It has often happened that the Catholic priest has left the service of the altar to take his place among the governing powers of society, and to enter the civil gradations of men. This religious influence has sometimes been used to secure the interests of the political order to which he belonged. At other times Catholics have sided with aristocracy out of religious feeling.

But as soon as the priesthood is entirely separated from the government, as is the case in the United States, no class of men is found more naturally disposed than the Catholics to carry the doctrine of the equality of conditions into the political world. If, then, the Catholic citizens of the United States are not forcibly led by the nature of their beliefs to adopt democratic and republican principles, at least they are not necessarily opposed to them; and their social position, as well as their small numbers, compels them to adopt these opinions. Most of the Catholics are poor, and they have no chance of taking part in government unless it is open to all citizens. They are a minority, and all rights must be respected in order to secure them the free exercise of their own. These two causes lead them, unconsciously, to adopt political doctrines that they would perhaps support with less zeal if they were rich and dominant.

The Catholic clergy of the United States has never attempted to oppose this political tendency; it seeks rather to justify its results. The priests in America have divided the intellectual world into two parts: in the one they place the doctrines of revealed religion, which command their assent; in the other they leave the truths they believe have been freely left open to political inquiry. Thus the Catholics of the United States are at once the most faithful believers and the most zealous citizens.

It may be said that in the United States no religious doctrine shows the slightest hostility to democratic and republican institutions. The clergy of all the different sects speak the same language; their opinions are in tune with the laws; and the human intellect flows onward in a single current.

I happened to be staying in one of the largest towns in the Union when I was invited to attend a public meeting called for the purpose of helping the Poles, and of sending them supplies of arms and money. I found two or three thousand people gathered in a vast hall prepared to receive them. After a short time a priest in his ecclesiastical robes stepped to the front of the platform: the spectators rose and stood bareheaded while he spoke in the following terms:—

"Almighty God! God of Armies! Thou who didst strengthen the hearts and guide the arms of our fathers when they fought for the sacred rights of national independence; Thou who didst make them triumph over a hateful oppression, and hast granted our people the benefits of liberty and peace: turn, O Lord, a favorable eye upon the other hemisphere; look down with pity upon that heroic nation which is even now struggling as we did in former times, and for the same rights we defended with our blood. Thou who didst create Man in the likeness of the same image, let not tyranny mar Thy work and establish inequality upon the earth. Almighty God! watch over the destiny of the Poles, and make them worthy to be free. May Thy wisdom direct their councils, and may Thy strength sustain their arms! Shed forth Thy terror upon their enemies, scatter the powers that take counsel against them, and grant that the injustice the world has witnessed for fifty years may not be consummated in our time. O Lord, who holdest alike the hearts of nations and of men in Thy powerful hand: raise up allies to the sacred cause of right; rouse the French nation from the apathy in which its rulers hold it, so that it may go forth again to fight for the liberties of the world.

"Lord, turn not Thy face from us, and grant that we may always be the most religious as well as the freest people of the earth. Almighty God, hear our supplications this day. Save the Poles, we beseech Thee, in the name of Thy well-beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who died upon the cross for the salvation of men. Amen."
The whole meeting responded "Amen!" with devotion.
Indirect Influence of Religious Opinions on Political Society in the United States

Christian morality common to all sects—Influence of religion on the manners of the Americans—Respect for the marriage tie—How religion confines the imagination of the Americans within certain limits and checks the passion for innovation—Opinion of the Americans on the political usefulness of religion—Their efforts to extend and secure its predominance.

I have just shown what the direct influence of religion on politics is in the United States, but its indirect influence appears to me to be even greater, and it never instructs the Americans more fully in the art of being free than when it says nothing about freedom.

The sects in the United States are innumerable. They all differ as to the worship due from man to his Creator, but they all agree as to the duties man owes to man. Each sect worships the Deity in its own particular way, but every sect preaches the same moral law in the name of God. If it is of the highest importance to man as an individual that his religion should be true, it is not the same with society. Society has no future life to hope for or to fear; and provided the citizens profess a religion, the particular tenets of that religion are of very little importance to its interests. Moreover, almost all the sects of the United States fall within the great unity of Christianity, and Christian morality is everywhere the same.

It may reasonably be believed that a certain number of Americans follow a particular form of worship from habit more than from conviction. In the United States the sovereign authority is religious, and so hypocrisy must be common; but there is no country in the whole world in which the Christian religion retains a greater influence over the souls of men than in America; and there can be no greater proof of its usefulness, and of its fit with human nature, than that its influence is most powerfully felt in the most enlightened and free nation on earth.

I have noted that the members of the American clergy in general, without even excepting those who do not admit religious liberty, are all in favor of civil freedom; but they do not support any particular political system. They keep aloof from parties and from public affairs. In the United States, religion exerts little influence on the laws or on the details of public opinion, but it directs the manners of the community, and by regulating domestic life it regulates the State.

I do not doubt that the great austerity of manners noticeable in the United States arises, in the first instance, from religious faith. Religion is often unable to restrain man from the countless temptations of fortune, nor can it check the passion for gain that every incident of his life contributes to arouse; but its influence on the mind of woman is supreme, and women are the protectors of morals. There is certainly no country in the world where the marriage tie is so much respected as in America, or where conjugal happiness is more highly or worthily valued. In Europe, almost all the disturbances of society arise from the irregularities of domestic life. To despise the natural bonds and legitimate pleasures of home is to contract a taste for excess, a restlessness of heart, and the evil of shifting desires. Stirred by the tumultuous passions that often disturb his home, the European is galled by the obedience the legislative powers of the State demand. But when the American retires from the turmoil of public life to the bosom of his family, he finds there the image of order and of peace. There his pleasures are simple and natural, his joys innocent and calm; and since he finds that an orderly life is the surest path to happiness, he accustoms himself without difficulty to moderating his opinions as well as his tastes. While the European tries to forget his domestic troubles by agitating society, the American draws from his own home that love of order which he afterwards carries with him into public affairs.

In the United States the influence of religion is not limited to manners—it extends to the intelligence of the people. Among the Anglo-Americans there are some who profess the doctrines of Christianity from sincere belief, and others who do so because they are afraid of being suspected of unbelief. Christianity therefore reigns without obstacle, by universal consent; and the consequence is, as I have already observed, that every principle of the moral world is fixed and determinate, even though the political world is left to the debates and experiments of men. Thus the human mind is never left to wander across a boundless field; and whatever its pretensions, it is checked from time to time by barriers it cannot cross. Before it can innovate, certain primal and unchanging principles are laid down, and the boldest conceptions of human design are subjected to certain forms that slow and halt their completion.

The imagination of the Americans, even in its greatest flights, is cautious and hesitant; its impulses are checked, its works unfinished. These habits of restraint recur in political society and are remarkably favorable both to the tranquility of the people and to the durability of the institutions it has established. Nature and circumstances combined to make the inhabitants of the United States bold men, as is sufficiently attested by the enterprising spirit with which they pursue fortune. If the American mind were free of all restraints, they would very shortly become the most daring innovators and the most implacable disputants in the world. But the revolutionaries of America are obliged to profess an outward respect for Christian morality and equity, which does not easily allow them to violate the laws that stand in the way of their designs; nor would they find it easy to overcome the scruples of their supporters, even if they were able to overcome their own. So far, no one in the United States has dared to advance the maxim that everything is permitted in the interest of society—an impious adage that seems to have been invented in an age of freedom to shelter all the tyrants of future ages. Thus, while the law permits the Americans to do what they please, religion prevents them from conceiving, and forbids them to commit, what is rash or unjust.

Religion in America takes no direct part in the government of society, but it must nevertheless be regarded as the foremost of the political institutions of that country; for if it does not give a taste for freedom, it makes the use of free institutions easier. Indeed, it is from this very point of view that the inhabitants of the United States themselves look upon religious belief. I do not know whether all Americans have a sincere faith in their religion—for who can search the human heart?—but I am certain that they hold it to be indispensable to the maintenance of republican institutions. This opinion does not belong to one class of citizens or to one party; it belongs to the whole nation, to every rank of society.

In the United States, if a political figure attacks a sect, this may not prevent even the supporters of that same sect from backing him; but if he attacks all the sects together, everyone abandons him, and he is left alone.

While I was in America, a witness who happened to be called at the assizes of the county of Chester (State of New York) declared that he did not believe in the existence of God or in the immortality of the soul. The judge refused to admit his testimony, on the ground that the witness had already destroyed all the Court's confidence in what he was about to say. *e The newspapers reported the fact without any further comment.

e [ The New York Spectator of August 23, 1831, relates the fact in the following terms:—"The Court of Common Pleas of Chester county (New York) a few days since rejected a witness who declared his disbelief in the existence of God. The presiding judge remarked that he had not before been aware that there was a man living who did not believe in the existence of God; that this belief constituted the sanction of all testimony in a court of justice, and that he knew of no cause in a Christian country where a witness had been permitted to testify without such belief."]

The Americans combine the notions of Christianity and of liberty so intimately in their minds that it is impossible to make them conceive one without the other; and with them this conviction does not spring from that barren traditionary faith that seems to vegetate in the soul rather than to live.

I have known of societies formed by the Americans to send ministers of the Gospel out into the new Western States to found schools and churches there, lest religion be allowed to die away in those remote settlements and the rising States be less fit to enjoy free institutions than the people from which they had come. I met wealthy New Englanders who abandoned the country in which they were born in order to lay the foundations of Christianity and of freedom on the banks of the Missouri, or in the prairies of Illinois. Thus religious zeal is perpetually stimulated in the United States by the duties of patriotism. These men do not act from an exclusive consideration of the promises of a future life; eternity is only one motive of their devotion to the cause; and if you converse with these missionaries of Christian civilization, you will be surprised to find how much value they set on the goods of this world—you meet a politician where you expected to find a priest. They will tell you that "all the American republics are collectively bound up with each other; if the republics of the West were to fall into anarchy, or to be mastered by a despot, the republican institutions that now flourish on the shores of the Atlantic Ocean would be in great peril. It is therefore in our interest that the new States should be religious, in order to maintain our liberties."

Such are the opinions of the Americans; and if anyone holds that the religious spirit I admire is the very thing most amiss in America, and that all that is missing for the freedom and happiness of the human race is to believe in some blind cosmogony, or to assert with Cabanis that thought is a secretion of the brain, I can only reply that those who speak this way have never been in America, and that they have never seen a religious or a free nation. When they return from their expedition, we shall hear what they have to say.

There are people in France who regard republican institutions as a temporary means to power, wealth, and distinction—men who are the condottieri of liberty, and who fight for their own advantage whatever the colors they wear. It is not to them that I am speaking. But there are others who look forward to the republican form of government as a calm and lasting state, toward which modern society is daily pushed by the ideas and manners of the time, and who sincerely wish to prepare men to be free. When these men attack religious opinions, they obey the dictates of their passions to the prejudice of their interests. Despotism may govern without faith, but liberty cannot. Religion is far more necessary in the republic they paint in glowing colors than in the monarchy they attack; and it is more needed in democratic republics than in any others. How is it possible that society should escape destruction if the moral tie is not tightened in proportion as the political tie is loosened? And what can be done with a people that is its own master, if it is not submissive to the Divinity?

Principal Causes That Make Religion Powerful in America: Care taken by the Americans to separate Church and State—The laws, public opinion, and even the efforts of the clergy combine to promote this end—Influence of religion on the mind in the United States attributable to this cause—Reason for this—What is the natural state of men with regard to religion at the present time—What are the peculiar and incidental causes that prevent men, in certain countries, from reaching this state.

The philosophers of the eighteenth century explained the gradual decay of religious faith in a very simple way. Religious zeal, they said, must necessarily fall as liberty is more widely established and knowledge more widely spread. Unfortunately, the facts are by no means in agreement with their theory. There are certain populations in Europe whose unbelief is matched only by their ignorance and debasement, while in America one of the freest and most enlightened nations in the world fulfills all the outward duties of religious fervor.

On my arrival in the United States, the religious aspect of the country was the first thing that struck my attention; and the longer I stayed there, the more I perceived the great political consequences flowing from this state of things, to which I was unaccustomed. In France I had almost always seen the spirit of religion and the spirit of freedom following courses diametrically opposed to each other; but in America I found them intimately united, reigning together over the same country. My desire to discover the causes of this phenomenon increased from day to day. To satisfy it, I questioned the members of all the different sects, and I more especially sought the company of the clergy, who are the depositaries of the different persuasions and who are most concerned for their endurance. As a member of the Roman Catholic Church, I was brought particularly into contact with several of its priests, with whom I became intimately acquainted. To each of these men I expressed my astonishment and explained my doubts; I found that they differed only on matters of detail, and that they attributed the peaceful dominion of religion in their country chiefly to the separation of Church and State. I do not hesitate to affirm that during my stay in America I did not meet a single individual, of the clergy or of the laity, who was not of the same opinion on this point.

This led me to examine more attentively than I had before the place the American clergy occupies in political society. I learned with surprise that they fill no public appointments; *f not one of them is to be met with in the administration, and they are not even represented in the legislative assemblies. In several States *g the law excludes them from political life, public opinion in all. And when I came to inquire into the prevailing spirit of the clergy, I found that most of its members seem to retire of their own accord from the exercise of power, and that they make it a point of professional pride to abstain from politics.
f [ Unless this term be applied to the functions which many of them fill in the schools. Almost all education is entrusted to the clergy.]

I heard them inveigh against ambition and deceit, under whatever political opinions these vices might lurk; but I learned from their discourses that in the eye of God men are not guilty for any opinions concerning political government they may profess sincerely, any more than they are for their mistakes in building a house or driving a furrow. I saw that these ministers of the gospel shunned all parties with the care that attends personal interest. These facts convinced me that what I had been told was true; and it then became my aim to investigate their causes, and to inquire how it happened that the real authority of religion was increased by a state of things that diminished its apparent force. These causes did not long escape my inquiry.

The short span of threescore years can never content the imagination of man, nor can the imperfect joys of this world satisfy his heart. Man alone, of all created beings, shows a natural contempt of existence and yet a boundless desire to exist; he scorns life, but he dreads annihilation. These different feelings ceaselessly drive his soul toward the contemplation of a future state, and religion directs his musings there. Religion, then, is simply another form of hope, and it is no less natural to the human heart than hope itself. Men cannot abandon their religious faith without a kind of mental aberration and a sort of violent distortion of their true natures; but they are inevitably brought back to more pious sentiments—for unbelief is an accident, and faith is the only permanent state of mankind. If we consider religious institutions only from a purely human point of view, they may be said to draw an inexhaustible element of strength from man himself, since they belong to one of the constituent principles of human nature.

I am aware that at certain times religion may reinforce this influence, which originates in itself, by the artificial power of the laws and the support of the temporal institutions that direct society. Religions closely united to the governments of the earth have been known to exercise a sovereign authority drawn from the twofold source of terror and faith; but when a religion enters into an alliance of this kind, I do not hesitate to affirm that it commits the same error as a man who would sacrifice his future to his present welfare. In obtaining a power to which it has no claim, it risks the authority that is rightfully its own. When a religion founds its empire on the desire for immortality that lives in every human heart, it may aspire to universal dominion; but when it links itself with a government, it must necessarily adopt maxims that apply only to certain nations. Thus, by forming an alliance with a political power, religion increases its authority over a few and forfeits the hope of reigning over all.

As long as a religion rests on those sentiments that are the consolation of all affliction, it may win the affections of mankind. But if it is mixed up with the bitter passions of the world, it may be forced to defend allies whom its interests, and not the principle of love, have given to it; or to push away as opponents men who are still attached to its own spirit, however opposed they may be to the powers with which it is allied. The Church cannot share the temporal power of the State without also becoming the object of a portion of the hostility that the latter provokes.

The political powers that seem most firmly established often have no better guarantee of their duration than the opinions of a generation, the interests of the time, or the life of an individual. A law can modify the social condition that seems most fixed and determinate; and with the social condition, everything else must change. The powers of society are more or less fleeting, like the years we spend on earth; they succeed one another rapidly, like the passing cares of life; and no government has ever yet been founded on an unchanging disposition of the human heart or on an imperishable interest.

As long as a religion is sustained by those feelings, tendencies, and passions that recur in the same forms at every period of history, it may defy the efforts of time; at the very least, it can be destroyed only by another religion. But when religion clings to the interests of the world, it becomes almost as fragile a thing as the powers of the earth. It is the only one of them all that can hope for immortality; but if it is bound to their ephemeral authority, it shares their fortunes and may fall with the transient passions that supported them for a day. The alliance a religion contracts with political powers is bound to be a burden to it, since it does not need their help to live, and by giving them its own help it exposes itself to decay.

The danger I have just pointed out always exists, but it is not always equally visible. In some ages governments seem imperishable; in others, the existence of society appears more precarious than the life of a man. Some constitutions plunge the citizens into a lethargic drowsiness, others rouse them to feverish excitement. When governments appear so strong and laws so stable, men do not perceive the dangers that may come from a union of Church and State. When governments display so much weakness and laws so much inconstancy, the danger is self-evident, but it is no longer possible to avoid it; to be effective, measures must be taken to detect its approach.

In proportion as a nation takes on a democratic social condition, and as communities show democratic tendencies, it becomes more and more dangerous to connect religion with political institutions. For the time is coming when authority will be passed from hand to hand, when political theories will follow one another, and when men, laws, and constitutions will disappear or be modified from day to day—and this, not for a season only, but unceasingly. Agitation and changefulness are inherent in the nature of democratic republics, just as stagnation and inertness are the law of absolute monarchies.

If the Americans—who change the head of the Government once in four years, who elect new legislators every two years, and renew the provincial officers every twelvemonth—if the Americans, who have abandoned the political world to the attempts of innovators, had not placed religion beyond their reach, where could it abide in the ebb and flow of human opinions? Where would the respect that is its due be paid, amid the struggles of faction? And what would become of its immortality, in the midst of perpetual decay? The American clergy were the first to perceive this truth, and to act accordingly. They saw that they must give up their religious influence if they were to strive for political power; and they chose to give up the support of the State rather than share its vicissitudes.

In America, religion is perhaps less powerful than it has been at certain periods in the history of certain peoples; but its influence is more lasting. It confines itself to its own resources, but of those none can deprive it: its circle is limited to certain principles, but those principles are entirely its own, and under its undisputed control.

On every side in Europe we hear voices complaining of the absence of religious faith, and asking the means of restoring to religion some remnant of its original authority. It seems to me that we must first consider carefully what the natural state of men with regard to religion ought to be at the present time; and when we know what we have to hope and to fear, we may discern the end toward which our efforts should be directed.

The two great dangers that threaten the existence of religions are schism and indifference. In ages of fervent devotion, men sometimes abandon their religion, but they only cast it off in order to adopt another. Their faith changes the objects to which it is directed, but it suffers no decline. The old religion then excites enthusiastic attachment in one party and bitter enmity in the other; some leave it with anger, others cling to it with increased devotedness; and although persuasions differ, irreligion is unknown. Such, however, is not the case when a religious belief is secretly undermined by doctrines that may be called negative, since they deny the truth of one religion without affirming that of any other. Prodigious revolutions then take place in the human mind, without the apparent cooperation of human passions, and almost without man's knowledge. Men lose the objects of their fondest hopes, as if by forgetfulness. They are carried away by an imperceptible current that they have not the courage to stem, but which they follow with regret, since it bears them from a faith they love to a skepticism that plunges them into despair.

In ages that match this description, men desert their religious opinions from lukewarmness rather than from dislike; they do not reject them, but the sentiments that once nourished them disappear. But even if the unbeliever does not admit religion to be true, he still considers it useful. Looking at religious institutions from a human point of view, he acknowledges their influence on manners and on legislation. He admits that they may serve to make men live in peace with one another, and to prepare them gently for the hour of death. He regrets the faith he has lost; and since he is deprived of a treasure whose full value he has come to appreciate, he scruples to take it from those who still possess it.

On the other hand, those who continue to believe are not afraid to avow their faith openly. They look upon those who do not share their conviction as more deserving of pity than of opposition; and they are aware that to gain the esteem of unbelievers they are not obliged to follow their example. They are hostile to no one in the world; and since they do not regard the society in which they live as an arena in which religion is bound to face its thousand deadly foes, they love their contemporaries even as they condemn their weaknesses and lament their errors.

Since those who do not believe conceal their incredulity, and those who believe display their faith, public opinion declares itself in favor of religion: love, support, and honor are bestowed upon it, and only by searching the human soul can one detect the wounds it has received. The mass of mankind, which is never without religious feeling, sees nothing at variance with the established faith. The instinctive desire for a future life brings the crowd around the altar, and opens the hearts of men to the precepts and consolations of religion.

But this picture does not apply to us. Among us there are men who have stopped believing in Christianity without adopting any other religion; others who are in the perplexities of doubt, and who already make a show of not believing; and others still who are afraid to avow the Christian faith that they still cherish in secret.

Amid these lukewarm partisans and ardent antagonists a small number of believers exist, ready to brave all obstacles and to scorn all dangers in defense of their faith. They have done violence to human weakness in order to rise above public opinion. Stirred up by the effort they have made, they hardly know where to stop; and since they know that the first use the French made of independence was to attack religion, they look upon their contemporaries with dread, and they recoil in alarm from the liberty their fellow-citizens are trying to obtain. Because unbelief seems to them a novelty, they lump together everything new in one indiscriminate animosity. They are at war with their age and country, and they look upon every opinion put forward there as the necessary enemy of the faith.

This is not the natural state of men with regard to religion at the present day; some extraordinary or incidental cause must be at work in France to prevent the human mind from following its original tendencies and to drive it beyond the limits at which it ought naturally to stop. I am deeply convinced that this extraordinary and incidental cause is the close connection between politics and religion. The unbelievers of Europe attack the Christians as their political opponents rather than as their religious adversaries; they hate the Christian religion as the opinion of a party far more than as an error of belief; and they reject the clergy less because they are the representatives of the Divinity than because they are the allies of authority.

In Europe, Christianity has been intimately united to the powers of the earth. Those powers are now in decay, and religion is, as it were, buried under their ruins. The living body of religion has been bound to the dead corpse of a superannuated polity: cut but the bonds that hold it, and that which is alive will rise once more. I do not know what could restore the Christian Church of Europe to the energy of its earlier days; that power belongs to God alone. But it may be the effect of human policy to leave the faith in the full exercise of the strength that still remains to it.
How the Instruction, the Habits, and the Practical Experience of the Americans Promote the Success of Their Democratic Institutions

What is to be understood by the instruction of the American people—The human mind more superficially instructed in the United States than in Europe—No one completely uninstructed—Reason for this—Rapidity with which opinions are diffused even in the uncultivated States of the West—Practical experience more useful to the Americans than book-learning.
I have very little to add to what I have already said about the influence that the instruction and habits of the Americans exert on the maintenance of their political institutions.

America has so far produced very few writers of distinction; it has no great historians, and not a single eminent poet. The inhabitants of that country regard what are properly called literary pursuits with a kind of disapproval; and there are second-rate towns in Europe in which more literary works are published each year than in the twenty-four States of the Union put together. The spirit of the Americans is averse to general ideas, and does not seek theoretical discoveries. Neither politics nor manufactures direct them to such occupations; and although new laws are continually being enacted in the United States, no great writers have yet inquired into the general principles of their legislation. The Americans have lawyers and commentators, but no jurists; *h and they furnish examples rather than lessons to the world. The same remark applies to the mechanical arts. In America, the inventions of Europe are adopted with sagacity; they are perfected, and adapted with admirable skill to the needs of the country. Manufactures exist, but the science of manufacture is not cultivated; they have good workmen, but very few inventors. Fulton was obliged to offer his services to foreign nations for a long time before he was able to devote them to his own country.
h [ [This cannot be said with truth of the country of Kent, Story, and Wheaton.]]

The observer who wishes to form an opinion on the state of instruction among the Anglo-Americans must consider the same object from two different points of view. If he singles out only the learned, he will be astonished to find how rare they are; but if he counts the ignorant, the American people will appear to be the most enlightened community in the world. The whole population, as I observed elsewhere, stands between these two extremes. In New England, every citizen receives the elementary notions of human knowledge; he is also taught the doctrines and the evidences of his religion, the history of his country, and the leading features of its Constitution. In Connecticut and Massachusetts, it is extremely rare to find a man imperfectly acquainted with all these things, and a person wholly ignorant of them is a sort of phenomenon.

When I compare the Greek and Roman republics with these American States—the manuscript libraries of the former and their rude population with the innumerable journals and the enlightened people of the latter; when I remember all the attempts that are made to judge the modern republics by the help of those of antiquity, and to infer what will happen in our time from what took place two thousand years ago—I am tempted to burn my books, in order to bring nothing but new ideas to bear on so new a condition of society.

What I have said of New England must not, however, be applied without distinction to the whole Union; as we move westward or southward, the instruction of the people declines. In the States bordering the Gulf of Mexico, a certain number of individuals may be found, as in our own countries, who lack the rudiments of instruction. But there is not a single district in the United States sunk in complete ignorance, and for a very simple reason: the peoples of Europe started from the darkness of a barbarous condition to advance toward the light of civilization; their progress has been unequal; some of them have improved rapidly, while others have loitered on their way, and some have stopped and are still sleeping beside it. *i

i [ [In the Northern States the number of persons destitute of instruction is inconsiderable, the largest number being 241,152 in the State of New York (according to Spaulding's Handbook of American Statistics for 1874); but in the South no less than 1,516,339 whites and 2,671,396 colored persons are returned as "illiterate."]]

This has not been the case in the United States. The Anglo-Americans settled in a state of civilization on the territory their descendants now occupy; they did not have to begin to learn, and it was enough for them not to forget. Now the children of these same Americans are the people who, year by year, carry their dwellings into the wilds—and with their dwellings, the knowledge they have acquired and their esteem for knowledge. Education has taught them the usefulness of instruction, and has enabled them to pass that instruction on to their posterity. In the United States, society has no infancy; it is born fully grown.

The Americans never use the word "peasant," because they have no idea of the particular class that term denotes; the ignorance of more remote ages, the simplicity of rural life, and the rusticity of the villager have not been preserved among them, and they are equally unacquainted with the virtues, the vices, the coarse habits, and the simple graces of an early stage of civilization. At the extreme borders of the Confederate States, on the edge of society and the wilderness, a population of bold adventurers has settled, who pierce the solitudes of the American woods and seek a country there in order to escape the poverty that awaited them in their native provinces. As soon as the pioneer reaches the spot that is to serve him as a refuge, he fells a few trees and builds a log house. Nothing could offer a more miserable aspect than these isolated dwellings. The traveler who approaches one of them toward nightfall sees the flicker of the hearth-flame through the chinks in the walls; and at night, if the wind rises, he hears the roof of boughs swaying to and fro amid the great forest trees. Who would not suppose that this poor hut is the asylum of rudeness and ignorance? Yet no sort of comparison can be drawn between the pioneer and the dwelling that shelters him. Everything about him is primitive and unformed, but he himself is the result of the labor and experience of eighteen centuries. He wears the dress and speaks the language of cities; he is acquainted with the past, curious about the future, and ready to argue about the present. He is, in short, a highly civilized being who consents, for a time, to inhabit the backwoods, and who penetrates the wilds of the New World with a Bible, an axe, and a file of newspapers.

It is difficult to imagine the incredible speed with which public opinion circulates in the midst of these deserts. *j I do not think that so much intellectual intercourse takes place in the most enlightened and populous districts of France. *k It cannot be doubted that, in the United States, the instruction of the people powerfully contributes to the support of a democratic republic; and such must always be the case, I believe, where instruction that awakens the understanding is not separated from moral education that amends the heart. But I by no means exaggerate this benefit, and I am still further from thinking, as so many people in Europe do, that men can be instantly made into citizens by teaching them to read and write. True information is mainly drawn from experience; and if the Americans had not been gradually accustomed to govern themselves, their book-learning would not help them much today.
