I have lived a great deal among the people in the United States, and I cannot express how much I admire their experience and good sense. An American should never be allowed to speak of Europe; for he will then probably display a great deal of presumption and very foolish pride. He will fall back on those crude and vague notions that are so useful to the ignorant all over the world. But if you question him about his own country, the cloud that dimmed his intelligence will immediately lift; his language will become as clear and precise as his thoughts. He will tell you what his rights are, and by what means he exercises them; he will be able to point out the customs that prevail in the political world. You will find that he is well acquainted with the rules of the administration, and that he is familiar with the mechanism of the laws. The citizen of the United States does not acquire his practical knowledge and his definite notions from books; the instruction he has acquired may have prepared him to receive those ideas, but it did not furnish them. The American learns the laws by taking part in the act of legislation, and he takes a lesson in the forms of government by governing. The great work of society is constantly going on before his eyes, and, as it were, under his hands.

In the United States, politics is the end and aim of education; in Europe its principal object is to fit men for private life. The participation of citizens in public affairs is too rare an occurrence to be anticipated in advance. A glance over society in the two hemispheres shows these differences even in its outward appearance.

In Europe we frequently introduce the ideas and habits of private life into public affairs; and since we pass at once from the domestic circle to the government of the State, we may often be heard discussing the great interests of society in the same manner in which we converse with our friends. The Americans, on the other hand, carry the habits of public life over into their manners in private; and in their country the jury is introduced into the games of schoolboys, and parliamentary forms are observed at the order of a feast.
The Laws Contribute More to the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States Than the Physical Circumstances of the Country, and the Manners More Than the Laws

All the nations of America have a democratic state of society—Yet democratic institutions subsist only among the Anglo-Americans—The Spaniards of South America, equally favored by physical causes as the Anglo-Americans, unable to maintain a democratic republic—Mexico, which has adopted the Constitution of the United States, in the same predicament—The Anglo-Americans of the West less able to maintain it than those of the East—Reason for these different results.

I have remarked that the maintenance of democratic institutions in the United States is due to the circumstances, the laws, and the manners of that country. *l Most Europeans know only the first of these three causes, and they are apt to give it a preponderating importance it does not really possess.
l [ I remind the reader of the general sense I give to the word "manners," namely, the moral and intellectual characteristics of social man taken collectively.]

It is true that the Anglo-Saxons settled in the New World in a state of social equality; the low-born and the noble were not to be found among them, and professional prejudices were always as entirely unknown as the prejudices of birth. Thus, since the condition of society was democratic, the empire of democracy was established without difficulty. But this circumstance is by no means peculiar to the United States; almost all the trans-Atlantic colonies were founded by men equal among themselves, or who became so by settling them. In no part of the New World have Europeans been able to create an aristocracy. Nevertheless, democratic institutions prosper nowhere but in the United States.

The American Union has no enemies to contend with; it stands in the wilds like an island in the ocean. But the Spaniards of South America were no less isolated by nature; yet their position has not spared them the burden of standing armies. They make war on each other when they have no foreign enemies to fight; and the Anglo-American democracy is the only one that has so far been able to maintain itself in peace. *m
m [ [A remark which, since the great Civil War of 1861-65, ceases to be applicable.]]

The territory of the Union offers a boundless field to human activity, and inexhaustible materials for industry and labor. The passion for wealth takes the place of ambition, and the heat of faction is tempered by a sense of prosperity. But in what part of the globe shall we find more fertile plains, mightier rivers, or more unexplored and inexhaustible riches than in South America?

Nevertheless, South America has been unable to maintain democratic institutions. If the welfare of nations depended on being placed in a remote position, with an unbounded stretch of habitable territory before them, the Spaniards of South America would have no reason to complain of their lot. And although they might enjoy less prosperity than the inhabitants of the United States, their condition might still be such as to excite the envy of some nations in Europe. Yet there are no nations on the face of the earth more miserable than those of South America.

Thus, not only are physical causes unable to produce results similar to those that occur in North America—they cannot even raise the population of South America above the level of European States, where they act in the opposite direction. Physical causes do not, therefore, affect the destiny of nations as much as has been supposed.

I have met men in New England who were on the point of leaving a country where they could have stayed in comfortable circumstances, in order to go seek their fortune in the wilds. Not far from that district I found a French population in Canada, crowded into a narrow territory although the same wilds were close at hand; and while the emigrant from the United States bought an extensive estate with the earnings of a short spell of labor, the Canadian paid as much for land as he would have paid in France. Nature offers the solitudes of the New World to Europeans, but they do not always know how to turn her gifts to account. Other peoples of America have the same physical conditions of prosperity as the Anglo-Americans, but without their laws and their manners; and these peoples are wretched. The laws and manners of the Anglo-Americans are therefore the effective cause of their greatness—the object of my inquiry.

I am far from supposing that the American laws are pre-eminently good in themselves; I do not hold them to be applicable to all democratic peoples, and several of them seem to me dangerous, even in the United States. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that American legislation, taken as a whole, is extremely well suited to the genius of the people and the nature of the country it is meant to govern. The American laws are therefore good, and to them must be attributed a large share of the success that attends the government of democracy in America; but I do not believe them to be the principal cause of that success. And if they seem to me to have more influence on the social happiness of the Americans than the nature of the country, there is, on the other hand, reason to believe that their effect is still less than that produced by the manners of the people.

The Federal laws are undoubtedly the most important part of the legislation of the United States. Mexico, which is no less fortunately situated than the Anglo-American Union, has adopted the same laws, yet is unable to accustom itself to the government of democracy. Some other cause is therefore at work, independently of the physical circumstances and the particular laws that enable democracy to rule in the United States.

Another still more striking proof may be offered. Almost all the inhabitants of the territory of the Union are descendants of a common stock; they speak the same language, they worship God in the same manner, they are affected by the same physical causes, and they obey the same laws. Where, then, do their characteristic differences come from? Why, in the Eastern States of the Union, does the republican government display vigor and regularity, and proceed with mature deliberation? Whence does it draw the wisdom and the durability that mark its acts, while in the Western States, on the contrary, society seems to be ruled by the powers of chance? There, public business is conducted with an irregularity and a passionate, feverish excitement that does not promise a long or sure duration.

I am no longer comparing the Anglo-American States to foreign nations; I am contrasting them with each other, and trying to discover why they are so unlike. The arguments drawn from the nature of the country and from differences in legislation are here all set aside. Recourse must be had to some other cause; and what other cause can there be, except the manners of the people?

It is in the Eastern States that the Anglo-Americans have been longest accustomed to the government of democracy, and that they have formed the habits and conceived the notions most favorable to its maintenance. Democracy has gradually penetrated their customs, their opinions, and the forms of social intercourse; it is found in all the details of daily life as much as in the laws. In the Eastern States, the instruction and practical education of the people have been most fully developed, and religion has been most thoroughly amalgamated with liberty. Now these habits, opinions, customs, and convictions are precisely the constituent elements of what I have called manners.

In the Western States, by contrast, a portion of these same advantages is still lacking. Many of the Americans of the West were born in the woods, and they mix the ideas and customs of savage life with the civilization of their parents. Their passions are more intense, their religious morality less authoritative, their convictions less secure. The inhabitants exercise no sort of control over their fellow-citizens, for they are scarcely acquainted with each other. The nations of the West show, to a certain extent, the inexperience and rude habits of a people in its infancy; for although they are made up of old elements, their assemblage is of recent date.

The manners of the Americans of the United States are, then, the real cause that makes that people the only one of the American nations able to sustain a democratic government; and it is the influence of manners that produces the different degrees of order and prosperity that may be distinguished in the several Anglo-American democracies. Thus the effect that the geographical position of a country may have on the duration of democratic institutions is exaggerated in Europe. Too much importance is attributed to legislation, too little to manners. These three great causes serve, no doubt, to regulate and direct the American democracy; but if they were to be ranked in their proper order, I should say that physical circumstances are less effective than the laws, and the laws very subordinate to the manners of the people. I am convinced that the most advantageous situation and the best possible laws cannot maintain a constitution in spite of the manners of a country; while the latter may turn the most unfavorable positions and the worst laws to some advantage. The importance of manners is a common truth to which study and experience incessantly direct our attention. It may be regarded as a central point in the range of human observation, and the common end of all inquiry. So seriously do I insist on this point that, if I have so far failed to make the reader feel the important influence which I attribute to the practical experience, the habits, the opinions—in short, to the manners of the Americans—on the maintenance of their institutions, I have failed in the principal object of my work.
Whether Laws and Manners Are Sufficient to Maintain Democratic Institutions in Other Countries Besides America

The Anglo-Americans, if transported into Europe, would be obliged to modify their laws—Distinction to be made between democratic institutions and American institutions—Democratic laws may be conceived better than, or at least different from, those the American democracy has adopted—The example of America only proves that it is possible to regulate democracy by the help of manners and legislation.

I have asserted that the success of democratic institutions in the United States is more intimately connected with the laws themselves and the manners of the people than with the nature of the country. But does it follow that the same causes would of themselves produce the same results if they were put into operation elsewhere? And if the country cannot adequately substitute for laws and manners, can laws and manners in turn substitute for the country? It will readily be understood that the elements necessary to answer this question are lacking: other peoples besides the Anglo-Americans are to be found in the New World, and as these peoples are affected by the same physical circumstances as the latter, they may fairly be compared with them. But there are no nations outside America that have adopted the same laws and manners while being destitute of the physical advantages peculiar to the Anglo-Americans. No standard of comparison therefore exists, and we can only venture an opinion on this subject.

It appears to me, in the first place, that a careful distinction must be made between the institutions of the United States and democratic institutions in general. When I reflect on the state of Europe, its mighty nations, its populous cities, its formidable armies, and the complex nature of its politics, I cannot suppose that even the Anglo-Americans, if they were transported to our hemisphere with their ideas, their religion, and their manners, could exist without considerably altering their laws. But a democratic nation may be imagined, organized differently from the American people. It is not impossible to conceive a government truly founded on the will of the majority—but one in which the majority, suppressing its natural leaning toward equality, should consent, for the sake of the order and stability of the State, to invest a family or an individual with all the prerogatives of the executive. A democratic society might exist in which the forces of the nation would be more centralized than they are in the United States; the people would exert a less direct and less irresistible influence on public affairs, and yet every citizen invested with certain rights would participate, within his sphere, in the conduct of the government. The observations I made among the Anglo-Americans lead me to believe that democratic institutions of this kind, prudently introduced into society so as gradually to mix with the habits and be interfused with the opinions of the people, might subsist in other countries besides America. If the laws of the United States were the only imaginable democratic laws, or the most perfect it is possible to conceive, I should admit that the success of those institutions affords no proof of the success of democratic institutions in general in a country less favored by natural circumstances. But since the laws of America appear to me to be defective in several respects, and since I can readily imagine others of the same general nature, the peculiar advantages of that country do not prove that democratic institutions cannot succeed in a nation less favored by circumstances, if it is ruled by better laws.

If human nature were different in America from what it is elsewhere, or if the social condition of the Americans generated among them habits and opinions different from those that arise from the same social condition in the Old World, the American democracies would offer no means of predicting what may happen in other democracies. If the Americans displayed the same propensities as all other democratic nations, and if their legislators had relied on the nature of the country and the favor of circumstances to hold those propensities within proper limits, the prosperity of the United States would be attributable exclusively to physical causes, and it would offer no encouragement to a people inclined to imitate their example without sharing their natural advantages. But neither of these suppositions is borne out by the facts.

In America the same passions are to be found as in Europe—some arising from human nature, others from the democratic condition of society. Thus in the United States I found that restlessness of heart which is natural to men when all ranks are nearly equal and the chances of advancement are the same for all. I found the democratic feeling of envy expressed in a thousand different forms. I observed that the people frequently displayed, in the conduct of affairs, a consummate mixture of ignorance and presumption, and I concluded that in America men are liable to the same failings and the same absurdities as among ourselves. But on examining the state of society more attentively, I soon discovered that the Americans had made great and successful efforts to counteract these imperfections of human nature, and to correct the natural defects of democracy. Their various municipal laws seemed to me a means of restraining the ambition of the citizens within a narrow sphere, and of turning those same passions which might have worked havoc in the State to the good of the township or the parish. The American legislators have succeeded to a certain extent in setting the notion of rights against the feelings of envy; the permanence of the religious world against the continual shifting of politics; the experience of the people against its theoretical ignorance; and its practical knowledge of business against the impatience of its desires.

The Americans, then, have not relied on the nature of their country to counterbalance the dangers arising from their Constitution and their political laws. To evils common to all democratic peoples they have applied remedies which none but themselves had ever thought of before; and although they were the first to make the experiment, they have succeeded in it.

The manners and laws of the Americans are not the only ones that may suit a democratic people; but the Americans have shown that it would be wrong to despair of regulating democracy by the help of manners and laws. If other nations should borrow this general and pregnant idea from the Americans, without, however, intending to imitate them in the particular application they have given it; if they should attempt to fit themselves for the social condition that it seems to be the will of Providence to impose upon the generations of this age, and so to escape from the despotism or the anarchy that threatens them—what reason is there to suppose that their efforts would not be crowned with success? The organization and establishment of democracy in Christendom is the great political problem of the time. The Americans, unquestionably, have not solved this problem, but they furnish useful data to those who undertake the task.
Importance of What Precedes with Respect to the State of Europe

It may readily be seen with what intention I undertook the foregoing inquiries. The question discussed here is interesting not only to the United States but to the whole world; it concerns not a nation but all mankind. If those nations whose social condition is democratic could remain free only so long as they inhabited the wilds, we could not but despair of the future destiny of the human race; for democracy is rapidly gaining a wider sway, and the wilds are gradually being peopled with men. If it were true that laws and manners are insufficient to maintain democratic institutions, what refuge would remain open to the nations but the despotism of a single individual? I am aware that there are many worthy people at the present time who are not alarmed at this latter alternative, and who are so tired of liberty as to be glad of repose, far from the storms that attend it. But these individuals are ill acquainted with the haven toward which they are bound. They are so deluded by their memories that they judge the tendency of absolute power by what it was in former times, and not by what it might become today.

If absolute power were re-established among the democratic nations of Europe, I am persuaded that it would take on a new form, and appear with features unknown to our forefathers. There was a time in Europe when the laws and the consent of the people had invested princes with almost unlimited authority; but they scarcely ever made use of it. I do not speak of the prerogatives of the nobility, of the authority of supreme courts of justice, of corporations and their chartered rights, or of provincial privileges, all of which served to break the blows of the sovereign authority and to keep a spirit of resistance alive in the nation. Apart from these political institutions—which, however opposed they may have been to personal liberty, served to keep the love of freedom alive in the public mind, and may be reckoned useful in this respect—the manners and opinions of the nation confined royal authority within barriers that were no less powerful for being less conspicuous. Religion, the affections of the people, the benevolence of the prince, the sense of honor, family pride, provincial prejudices, custom, and public opinion all limited the power of kings and restrained their authority within an invisible circle. The constitution of nations was despotic at that time, but their manners were free. Princes had the right, but they had neither the means nor the desire, of doing whatever they pleased.

But what now remains of the barriers that once arrested the aggressions of tyranny? Since religion has lost its empire over the souls of men, the most prominent boundary that divided good from evil has been overthrown; the very elements of the moral world are uncertain; the princes and the peoples of the earth are guided by chance, and none can define the natural limits of despotism or the bounds of license. Long revolutions have forever destroyed the respect that once surrounded the rulers of the State; and now that they have been relieved of the burden of public esteem, princes may henceforward surrender themselves without fear to the seductions of arbitrary power.

When kings find that the hearts of their subjects are turned toward them, they are clement, because they are conscious of their strength; and they are careful of their people's affection, because that affection is the bulwark of the throne. A mutual exchange of goodwill then takes place between the prince and the people, like the gracious intercourse of domestic society. The subjects may murmur at the sovereign's decree, but they are grieved to displease him; and the sovereign chastises his subjects with the light hand of parental affection.

But once the spell of royalty is broken in the tumult of revolution; when successive monarchs have passed across the throne, so as alternately to display to the people the weakness of their right and the harshness of their power—the sovereign is no longer regarded by any as the Father of the State, and is feared by all as its master. If he is weak, he is despised; if he is strong, he is detested. He himself is full of animosity and alarm; he finds himself a stranger in his own country, and he treats his subjects like conquered enemies.

When the provinces and the towns formed so many different nations within their common country, each of them had a will of its own, opposed to the general spirit of subjection; but now that all the parts of the same empire, after having lost their immunities, their customs, their prejudices, their traditions, and their names, are subjected and accustomed to the same laws, it is no more difficult to oppress them collectively than it was formerly to oppress them one by one.

While the nobles enjoyed their power, and indeed long after that power was lost, the honor of aristocracy conferred an extraordinary degree of force on their personal opposition. They provide instances of men who, despite their weakness, still held a high opinion of their personal worth, and dared to stand alone against the efforts of the public authority. But at the present day, when all ranks are more and more blurred together, when the individual disappears into the throng and is easily lost in a common obscurity, when the honor of monarchy has almost lost its empire without being succeeded by public virtue, and when nothing enables a man to rise above himself, who shall say at what point the demands of power and the servility of weakness will stop?

As long as family feeling was kept alive, the opponent of oppression was never alone; he looked around him and found his clients, his hereditary friends, and his kinsfolk. If this support was lacking, he was sustained by his ancestors and animated by his posterity. But when patrimonial estates are divided, and when a few years suffice to confound the distinctions of a race, where can family feeling be found? What force can there be in the customs of a country that has changed and is still perpetually changing its aspect—a country in which every act of tyranny has a precedent, and every crime an example; in which there is nothing so old that its antiquity can save it from destruction, and nothing so unparalleled that its novelty can prevent it from being done? What resistance can be offered by manners of so pliant a make that they have already often yielded? What strength can even public opinion retain when no twenty persons are connected by a common tie; when not a man, nor a family, nor a chartered corporation, nor a class, nor a free institution, has the power of representing or asserting that opinion; and when every citizen—being equally weak, equally poor, and equally dependent—has only his personal impotence to oppose to the organized force of the government?

The annals of France furnish nothing analogous to the condition into which that country might then be thrown. But it may more aptly be likened to the times of old, and to those hideous eras of Roman oppression, when the manners of the people were corrupted, their traditions obliterated, their habits destroyed, their opinions shaken, and freedom, expelled from the laws, could find no refuge in the land; when nothing protected the citizens, and the citizens no longer protected themselves; when human nature was the sport of man, and princes wearied out the clemency of Heaven before they exhausted the patience of their subjects. Those who hope to revive the monarchy of Henry IV or of Louis XIV appear to me to be afflicted with mental blindness; and when I consider the present condition of several European nations—a condition toward which all the others tend—I am led to believe that they will soon be left with no other alternative than democratic liberty or the tyranny of the Caesars. *n
n [ [This prediction of the return of France to imperial despotism, and of the true character of that despotic power, was written in 1832, and realized to the letter in 1852.]]

And indeed it is worth considering whether men are to be entirely emancipated or entirely enslaved; whether their rights are to be made equal, or wholly taken away from them. If the rulers of society were reduced either to raise the crowd gradually to their own level, or to sink the citizens below that of humanity, would not the doubts of many be resolved, the consciences of many be healed, and the community prepared to make great sacrifices with little difficulty? In that case, the gradual growth of democratic manners and institutions should be regarded, not as the best, but as the only means of preserving freedom; and without liking the government of democracy, it might be adopted as the most applicable and the fairest remedy for the present ills of society.

It is difficult to associate a people in the work of government; but it is still more difficult to supply it with experience and to inspire in it the feelings it needs in order to govern well. I grant that the caprices of democracy are perpetual; its instruments are rough; its laws imperfect. But if it were true that soon no middle ground would exist between the empire of democracy and the dominion of a single arm, should we not rather incline toward the former than submit voluntarily to the latter? And if complete equality is to be our fate, is it not better to be leveled by free institutions than by despotic power?

Those who, after reading this book, should imagine that my intention in writing it has been to propose the laws and manners of the Anglo-Americans for the imitation of all democratic peoples, would be making a very great mistake; they must have paid more attention to the form than to the substance of my ideas. My aim has been to show, by the example of America, that there may exist laws, and especially manners, that will allow a democratic people to remain free. But I am very far from thinking that we ought to follow the example of the American democracy, and copy the means it has used to attain its ends; for I am well aware of the influence that the nature of a country and its political precedents exert on a constitution, and I should regard it as a great misfortune for mankind if liberty were to exist all over the world under the same forms.

But I am of the opinion that if we do not succeed in gradually introducing democratic institutions into France, and if we despair of imparting to the citizens those ideas and sentiments that first prepare them for freedom and afterward allow them to enjoy it, there will be no independence at all—neither for the middling classes nor the nobility, for the poor nor the rich—but an equal tyranny over all; and I foresee that if the peaceable empire of the majority is not founded among us in time, we shall sooner or later arrive at the unlimited authority of a single despot.
